claims.text: Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi has relatively low hardness and strength despite excellent plasticity and machinability.
The relatively low hardness and strength of CoCrFeNiTi are governed by a simple solid-solution microstructure lacking nanoscale precipitates.
In precipitation-free CoCrFeNiTi, dislocations move relatively freely.
Relatively free dislocation motion gives CoCrFeNiTi good ductility but low resistance to plastic flow.
Relatively free dislocation motion accounts for the machinability of CoCrFeNiTi.
The starting equimolar or near-equimolar CoCrFeNiTi is a single-phase FCC or BCC solid solution without secondary precipitates.
Thermal aging near 600 °C can induce a uniform dispersion of nanoscale precipitates in equimolar CoCrFeNiTi.
The aging treatment can nucleate and grow fine precipitates without dissolving the matrix.
Nanoscale precipitates act as obstacles to dislocation motion through precipitation strengthening.
Aged, precipitation-containing CoCrFeNiTi will have greater hardness than the as-cast precipitation-free alloy.
Aged, precipitation-containing CoCrFeNiTi will have greater yield or compressive strength than the as-cast precipitation-free alloy.
Precipitation strengthening may reduce the ductility of CoCrFeNiTi.
The proposed comparison applies at room temperature and up to 600 °C under controlled loading conditions.
The exact improvements in hardness and yield strength and the reduction in ductility cannot be predicted without experimental calibration.
Failure to form precipitates despite aging would falsify the claim that the absence of precipitates causes the low hardness and strength.

contradictions.description: The boundary says the alloy's simple solid-solution state is fixed, whereas the intervention is explicitly intended to create precipitates or secondary phases and therefore change that state.

The design requires confirmation that precipitates formed before mechanical comparison, but the rule also treats failure of the treatment to form precipitates as falsification of the causal hypothesis. Failure to manipulate the proposed mediator is not by itself a decisive test of its mechanical effect.
